title: New Swift packages add open-model choices for speech and decisions
dek: Two independent Swift libraries add selectable speech engines and typed model decisions, putting integration choices into application code.

sources.title: Bring advanced speech-to-text to your app with SpeechAnalyzer, WWDC25

lede: Developer Mattt introduced AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel on October 29, giving Swift applications new interfaces for speech recognition and model decisions. The packages let developers separate application logic from some model choices, while keeping responsibility for testing the resulting behavior.

body.heading: The speech baseline stays useful
body.text: Apple's SpeechAnalyzer already provides an on-device transcription path with system-managed model assets, as its WWDC25 session explains. AnySpeechRecognizer offers a familiar interface with additional engine choices. That makes Apple's implementation the closest practical baseline for a speech application. We would start a comparison with the same recording and the same output requirements. A team that only needs transcription should first establish what a different engine contributes. Speaker attribution, supported languages and useful timing information are better selection criteria than the mere availability of another backend.

body.heading: A shared interface has boundaries
body.text: The speech repository documents differences from Apple's framework, including its own analyzer and module types. An application cannot assume every native module fits unchanged into the package. The repository also supplies a command-line evaluation tool that reports transcription errors, elapsed time and memory. Our suggested adoption test is a small integration branch with one existing recording workflow. Keep audio capture, display and storage unchanged where possible. Then exercise cancellation and final results, because the interface must fit the application's lifecycle as well as its recognition needs.

body.heading: Match the engine to the screen
body.text: Mattt's launch post distinguishes Parakeet's live output and word timing from Qwen3-ASR's segment-final output. We would treat a live caption view and a completed recording viewer as separate product tests. In a caption view, delayed output changes how a user follows a conversation. In a recording viewer, final transcription quality may matter more. A shared API makes this comparison easier to organize; it does not settle it.

body.heading: Typed decisions remove one integration step
body.text: AnyDecisionModel exposes probabilities and typed choices or scores, with local and hosted backends documented in its repository. The developer can consume a defined result instead of extracting an answer from generated prose. For a hypothetical support queue, we would define the allowed destinations before connecting the model. We would also keep an explicit path for human review. The useful measurement would be whether messages reach the correct queue, including ambiguous messages that fit several categories. Successful parsing would only establish that the application received a usable data structure.

body.heading: Calibrate the decision you will deploy
body.text: The decision repository defines confidence as probability concentration for local answers and warns against comparisons across backends. Our evaluation plan would therefore keep a labeled test set separate from any calibration examples. It would report errors for each destination, not merely one combined score. We would inspect confident mistakes first, because those are the cases a threshold may send straight into an automated workflow. An application owner should decide the acceptable error cost before selecting that threshold.

body.heading: Keep the comparison reproducible
body.text: For deployment, we recommend recording the package revision, selected model and target device beside each result. Repeat the same inputs after a dependency update and retain the previous outputs for review. Test download failures and unavailable services alongside successful requests, since a fallback is part of the user experience. We would also compare the effort required to maintain each path. A slightly different transcript may be acceptable for a search index and unacceptable for a quotation tool. That distinction belongs in the application's acceptance criteria before the team chooses its default engine.

buildersNote: Run the speech evaluation tool on your target device using your own recordings. For decisions, reserve a separate labeled test set before fitting calibration, and record errors by output category before enabling automatic routing.

comparison.caption: Closest speech alternatives: Apple documentation and the package documentation describe different output contracts.

claims.text: The two independent packages were announced on October 29, 2026
The speech package documents Swift 6.2 and macOS 26 or iOS 26 requirements
The creator reports speech results from a Mac; the post does not establish iPhone performance
Typed decisions establish that an automated routing threshold is reliable
Hosted compatibility is tested with fixtures; calibration transfer beyond the tested tasks is unestablished

ourRead: We favor these packages as a way to compare application behavior without rewriting every integration. The strongest case is a specific missing feature, such as speaker attribution or typed routing output. We would keep the native speech path in the evaluation and avoid a blanket migration. Repeated target-device tests showing lower maintenance effort and fewer application-level errors would change our mind about making the new path the default.
watching: On November 7, 2026, we will revisit the speech repository for iPhone evaluations and any changes to documented engine capabilities.
On November 7, 2026, we will check whether the decision repository adds live hosted-service tests or new calibration evidence.
